utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. I gather, Ms. Somers, there's some matter to be raised.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to raise what I suppose is more of an administrative but really it affects the practice matter. At the beginning of the Defence case, the Prosecution indicated that -- and of course the Chamber is well aware -- the arrival of information about the witnesses comes extremely late, and it comes sometimes hours before midnight on the day before or the night before, which was the situation last night as to the witness after the current witness. And I am not clear how to find a solution to it. I know that the Defence also has indicated to me it is experiencing enormous time pressures in the proofing process, and of course we have been receiving communications from the Defence on a fairly regular basis that this is what you can know so far. We have not yet proofed the witness. We'll let you know if any other matters will be gone into. In fact, that makes it very difficult if not impractical to prepare adequately for cross-examination on hours of notice. I had indicated earlier that from time to time we may be in a position to we have to seek deferral on cross-examination, depending -- we know almost next to nothing about the coming witness, the next witness. This present one also was somewhat of a surprise, and there's an issue I'd like to raise about that one as well. But this may cause a continued problem in our ability to have an effective or to prepare effectively for cross-examination. The second matter -- if the Chamber would like me to pause between matters, I will do so, or if you'd like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No. Pour it all out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. The subject matter of the witness presently on the stand was marginally -- part of it was marginally approached during the examination of Admiral Jokic. The -- I seem not to have this in my own folder. The page I have got -- I'm sorry, another folder. But it was never put to Admiral Jokic in any specific way that a particular telephone call or conversation may have occurred. We believe -- we find ourselves raising the spectre of 90(H)(ii) on a regular basis. We believe in this instance it is extremely poignant and at the issue -- I will, at the break, if I may be permitted, present where the reference was to any communications on the 6th between General Kadijevic and Admiral Jokic earlier in the day. The guts of the examination now focuses on an area that was not put to the admiral as one puts the case to the admiral. So I want to preserve that matter for any further submissions that the Prosecution may have to make. But I think the Chamber should be aware of that. It was on 14 April. That much I remember, and I apologise. I thought I had taken with me the particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the second matter, you say that may need to be raised again later. With respect to the first matter, is there any positive matter that you raise, or you are you just bringing this problem to the notice of the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is altogether possible, Your Honour, after hearing the testimony of today's -- the following witness, not the current one on the stand, the Prosecution may need to seek additional time to prepare for cross-examination. And wanted to give the Chamber notice of that in advance. We are concerned about the regularised practice of getting the information very, very, very late, and the generality of it and usually that proofing may yield other matters of which we will at some point be informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything, Mr. Rodic or Mr. Petrovic, that you wish to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, I want to point out that what my learned colleague has just said is true. Unfortunately, it is true. And the reason is that the circumstances under which we have been proofing our witnesses are such that we do not have sufficient time to forward information on the witnesses more ahead of time. We are doing all we can and we understand the problems faced by the OTP. I do, however, wish to say that our problems are considerably greater than theirs. We are doing our best, nonetheless. We are trying to prepare as much information as possible for them. We are pressing on ceaselessly, and whenever we receive information by fax or from our investigators, we forward the information to them. We submitted this set of information last night at 9.00. The proofing began at 1.00 and finished at 4.00 in the afternoon. We are doing our best, nevertheless; however, these are objective factors and we hope we can cope with these factors to the best of our ability. Most of the factual witnesses have already been examined and cross-examined without any considerable problems. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. The proofing began at 9.00 p.m. and finished at 1.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That last correction only adds emphasis to the fact that the proofing is being undertaken at an extremely late stage, and that is a significant part of the problem. The Defence case has been in preparation, no doubt, since before the commencement of the trial, and yet we hear of proofing of a witness the night before. And it's not just the matter of one isolated witness and a surprise issue that's necessitated bringing in an additional witness. It seems to be a pattern with all witnesses. We'll just have to make the best we can of it as it goes along, trying to keep a fair hand between each side. We'll have the witness in, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please be seated. If I could remind you of the affirmation you took at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies. Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Rodic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown document D96. Good morning, Mr. Handzijev. We shall proceed with our examination-in-chief. You have already seen this document, and what I would like you to do now is to turn to page 70. Can you please look at this entry at 1349 hours. That's the column where the time is recorded, 1349 hours. The entry in relation to that specific time.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says here that frigate Captain Handzijev was ordered to call Bileca and Trebinje and to order Captain Kovacevic [as interpreted] to come immediately to the forward command post of the military naval sector command?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Me. I don't know whether counsel said Captain Kovacevic or not, but the entry says Colonel Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did say colonel. I read exactly as it says here. I said colonel. I think it's probably an error in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Handzijev, if you remember, can you please tell us whether Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this message or this order to you was in fact carried out.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most probably it was carried out. Right now, I can't remember specifically. It is a minor order, in my opinion, and was probably carried out by my assistant. In any other case, I am sure the command would have reacted and requested for this to be done again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is my only remaining portion of my examination-in-chief, and this concludes my examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Ms. Somers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Handzijev.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the Chief of Staff in September 1991 in the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was Admiral Zec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until approximately 20th of September, 1991, who was the Chief of Staff in the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was Admiral Zec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Admiral Zec's predecessor?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: His predecessor. For a while, it was warship Captain Ivo Milisic. I think that's what his name was. He came from Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I'm not getting a translation. Maybe I'm -- would you repeat that for me, please.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think his name was Ivo Milisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... think about that for a minute. How long had you been working in the 9th VPS when Ivo -- and what is -- is Ivo a full name, a complete name, or does it stand for something else? Ivo Milisic was the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right now, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. When was the transition made between Ivo Milisic as Chief of Staff and Milan Zec as Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most probably when he was detained. Warship Captain Milisic, I mean. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Most probably when he was detained.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was battleship Captain Milisic detained? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since I appeared as witness at his trial and I was there for the entire proceedings, I can tell you that he was detained because he failed to carry out an order for mobilisation, an order given by Admiral Kandic. I'm entirely familiar with this case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the case that bears 211/91 out of the Nis military court that was started in 1991 and the appeal was finished in 1992? Are we talking about that case?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't give you the exact numbers or the years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did Captain Milisic want to stay in the JNA? Did he want to remain in the JNA at the time of the occurrences you just described?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I am entirely familiar with this case, with all its details. I remember it as though -- if it was yesterday. We were called before the operations began and before a decision on those operations was read out. We had been called, and the late battleship Captain Djurisic, or Djurovic, resolutely stated: "We are now going into the room, and in the room we shall hear the decision. Whoever is having second thoughts should not enter the room." "Once in the room, there's no going back." He said resolutely. I think my rendering of how it actually happened is quite accurate. And the person that we have already referred to, battleship Captain Milisic, he went into the room, and thereby agreed to stay with the JNA. Now, what his intentions were when he did it, that's not as clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity, Captain Milisic?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did he feel about the possibility of mobilisation? You expressed earlier how you felt about things. How did he feel about things? After all, you know him very well.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him really well. We're family of sorts. His wife's sister is married to a close relation of my wife. But we were on visiting terms. We were close. I knew what his personal position was on the matter, but I believe that he may have been wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why don't you tell us what his personal position was on the matter.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: He declared himself a Yugoslav at the time, or at least that's what he told me, and I couldn't feel that he was actually keeping something secret, because I trusted him very much. Maybe this was not his true position, but what he told me was that he felt a Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the proceeding that was lodged against Captain Milisic, a Croatian then Chief of Staff, involved charges of -- let's see. What were the charges that were levelled against the captain?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he received the order, I was standing a stone's throw from where he was. It was in the morning that General Kandic's order arrived. I was at the operational centre myself. And I heard everything that Kandic was ordering him, exactly which units he was supposed to mobilise. However, in the meantime, he had left for Trebinje, and the units were never mobilised. There was a huge number of artillery units. When our commander at the time, the person who was the commander of the 9th VPS at the time, or the 9th sector, came, he was in hospital. When he was back at hospital at half past 2.00 or 3.00, he called Kandic. I happen to be there at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the charges that were levelled against Captain Milisic? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember very clearly what the charges were. Probably sabotage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Probably sabotage. Any other charge?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, he was a good friend of yours, almost family?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. We used to see each other a lot. He would come to my place or we would go to see another relative, my wife's relative, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On 20th of September, 1991, did you provide information to investigators of a military tribunal claiming to have listened in on a telephone conversation between Admiral Kandic and the late Commander Djurovic?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I was even confronted with Kandic, and Kandic's statements were contradictory in court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you testified before a military court in Nis? You testified -- did you testify under oath? Did you give an oath when you testified?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure that applies is the same in all courts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified before a military court in Nis about the alleged conversation. So you listened in to a conversation between two high-ranking officers; is that correct? Is that how you gained the testimony?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this while --

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this while you were acting as a duty-officer in the 9th VPS? Is that how you listened in to the conversation?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember clearly --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... you can't remember?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection. My colleague is not allowing the witness to finish answering. Therefore, may he please be allowed to finish his sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness is not answering. That's the point. Counsel is bringing the witness back to the question. So carry on, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this while you were acting as a duty-officer in the 9th VPS that you overheard the conversation, was it a telephone conversation, between Admiral Kandic and Commander Djurovic?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Ivo Milisic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you testify about a conversation between Djurovic and Kandic, or Milisic and Kandic? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I testified and wrote a statement prior to that with respect to the conversation with Admiral Kandic and the conversation with Milisic, and I also testified about what I heard. And I answered the question, what I heard in connection with the conversation that was held later in the afternoon hours between Captain -- warship Captain Djurovic and Tadic [as interpreted]. So I answered those questions in court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were giving information -- you gave evidence against Captain Milisic and you represented certain --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting. But on page 11, line 10, it says Tadic. The name was Kandic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave evidence against Captain Milisic based on words you said Admiral Kandic spoke, that you claimed to have heard Admiral Kandic speak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what he said when he spoke about warship Captain Milisic or when he was speaking to Djurisic, Captain Djurovic. Would you please tell me that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could the last question be repeated. The answer is not exactly what the witness said in B/C/S. So would the -- would my learned colleague repeat what she said, because the witness did not say what it purports to say here on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I will repeat page 11, line 17. Question: You gave evidence against Captain Milisic based on words you said Admiral Kandic spoke, words that you claim to have heard Admiral Kandic speak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I exactly heard what Admiral Kandic ordered warship Captain Milisic to do, because I was one and a half metres away from him, and the speakerphone was switched on where I was the duty-officer. So the whole hall could have heard the same thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was while you were acting as a duty-officer in your official capacity in the 9th VPS; am I right on that? Did I get that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct. But I can't remember whether I was handing over my duty or taking over duty or whether I was just present as chief of the operations centre. I can't remember. But that's not the essential point. I was present, and when Kandic spoke with warship Captain Milisic, I was there, and later on when Kandic phoned warship Captain Djurovic. So that was 2.00 or 3.00 in the afternoon. So I heard it. I remember it and can remember the actual words that were uttered at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your training -- first of all, did you have training as a duty-officer or an operation centre officer?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: During our education at the academy, we have to go through all stages of training, all kinds of training and all the training for duty officers. And as a cadet, I was a guard for time, then I was commander of the guards. Then I was something that we call SIZ. That was duty. And then further up the line. Otherwise, I personally, when I took over my duties, we have to have studied all the documents regulating our service, all our branches and services and guidelines and instructions, pinpointing our duties. And then this is an ongoing process. We put it into practice, and when our superior officer deems that we are fully fit, then we can take up our duties ourselves without any supervision. So I passed through this entire process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, isn't it part of training to respect the secrecy, the confidentiality, the integrity of communications between officers, particularly of superior rank to yourself?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in moments of that kind, when faced with situations of that kind, and I was the chief of the operations centre, so when I was asked in court, I could not answer otherwise; otherwise, I would have deviated from court principles. Because I did hear the conversation. It was a public conversation. And if that warship Captain Milisic considered that it was confidential or secret, then he should have found a way of speaking without the rest of us hearing, just to lift up the receiver and not the speakerphone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... eavesdropping. Isn't that what you were doing? You were eavesdropping on a conversation that was not your conversation. You did not correctly have the terms of the conversation, and you then went on to relay what you claimed was said in the conversation. You simply eavesdropped, did you not?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that conversation, and it wasn't only I who heard it, but all the others who were witnesses to it. It was a public conversation. The whole hall and operations centre could hear it. So when I was asked in court were you present there? My answer was yes. Did you hear the conversation? I said yes. Should I have said that I did not when I did? Should I have said in court that I did not? What would you think of me if I were to lie in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the charge that was levelled, one of the charges levelled against Captain Milisic, the then Chief of Staff, as a result of your evidence, was a charge of subversion of military and defence capacities, pursuant Article 121, paragraph 1, of the Penal Code of the SFRY. Is that in your view a serious charge?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the most serious charge, whereas I did not accuse him. I just stated what I heard. And I would have felt far luckier had I not heard anything. My conscience would have been clear. But what can I do? I heard it and I couldn't keep it secret. I would have gladly kept it secret. It would have been easier for me to do so and all my relatives and friends wouldn't have spat at me. But that's the kind of man I am. I can't hide anything. I don't keep anything secret because my duty requires otherwise. How would courts be able to work if people hide relevant information?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you remember this incident as if it were today. Do you remember why the charge of subversion was dropped, was not sustained by the courts? Do you remember that, as concerning any communication between Admiral Kandic and Captain Milisic? Do you remember what the court said about that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You should have -- you should ask the court. But I know that he was charged and that afterwards he was sentenced to five years and then replaced. He was charged -- I didn't charge him. I didn't accuse him. I don't know what the court thinks. It's not my business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What he was convicted of ultimately was disobeying an order of Admiral Djurovic, not of Admiral Kandic. Do you want to tell us why he didn't disobey an order of Admiral Kandic and subvert the military in so doing, as you suggested by your evidence that you gave in that court?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of the fact that he refused to carry out Djurovic's orders, and I say 100 per cent certainty that Kandic ordered him that. So I don't like to lie. I don't like to fabricate things. Kandic said it and it's as if it were yesterday. I remember it clearly. Kandic ordered him -- it was only later that Djurovic, when he came, was informed of this. Kandic called him and said, "Djuro, did you carry out that order of mine?" And he said: "What order?" And he said: "What I issued -- the order I issued to Ivo." And he said: "That's the first I hear of it." And then Kandic said: "Oh, Djuro, your left shoe doesn't know what your right shoe is doing." Those were his very words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you have respect for the court system of your military at the time, of the JNA? Did you respect the decisions of the judges?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I respected the decisions of the judges. How wouldn't I? It's a ludicrous question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will read and ask you if you recall, since it was like yesterday -- first of all, what was your -- what is military -- Kumbor military post 4004? What is that? Where is that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the command, with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the same post --

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, but I'm not quite sure. I think that's it. But I don't remember those figures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long --

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: But yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. How long did you work -- had you been working at Kumbor as of September 20, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the -- from 1980.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't recall that the post number was 4004, after 11 years of service?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're just numbers. I changed a lot of those military posts. But yes, it probably was. But I'm not good at memorising figures, numbers. You know, once the virus enters the head. But yes, it was probably that post. I was -- had more connections with the command rather than the military post, so when I wrote orders or reports, I would title them "the command of the 9th VPS." So that was the important thing. I suppose it was our military post, but I don't see that it's essential what the figures actually were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the judgement of 30 March 1992 from the military court in Nis, it is above all necessary to point out that at the trial it was established on the basis of an analysis and assessment of navy command report 32-64, on 25 March 1992, and the report of the command of the Kumbor military post 4004, number 39-55-2 of 20 March 1992. It was established that in the said commands, there are no written or other traces of proof or the content of the telephone conversation conducted on 20 September 1991 between the witness Mile Kandic and the accused, the accused being Ivan or Ivo Milisic. In connection with this fact, the commander of the superior unit, the Split military post 5437, witness Mile Kandic said at the trial that he had not ordered the accused to mobilise units. On the other hand, witness Dusko Knezevic said that at the end of the telephone conversation with the accused, witness Mile Kandic told the accused to additionally mobilise other units. Witness Petre Handzijev said that he heard the telephone conversation conducted by witness Mile Kandic and witness Krsto Djurovic in the afternoon of 20 September 1991 and that witness Kandic asked Djurovic whether mobilisation had been carried out, to which Djurovic replied that he had taken measures but that his order had not been relayed to him and that witness Mile Kandic replied that he had issued the order or relayed it to Ivo during the morning. Finally, witness Krsto Djurovic said that around 1900 hours on 20 September 1991 he telephoned his commander witness Mile Kandic in connection with the need to mobilise units and that witness Kandic replied: "Didn't your deputy relay to you that I issued an order to you to mobilise everyone?" Witness Djurovic claims that according to what witness Mile Kandic told him, the accused received a mobilisation order from witness Mile Kandic. With respect to the situation described in existing evidence, and there is no other evidence, the court found that there was no reliable evidence that witness Mile Kandic ordered the accused Milisic to mobilise units because witness Kandic asserts categorically that he did not issue such an order to the accused, and he certainly is the one who knows this best. And with respect to this fact, he is the only authentic and direct witness, while all the other witnesses are not direct witness and have testified about what they heard from a telephone conversation between witness Mile Kandic and the accused. Knezevic, that is, from the telephone conversation between witness Mile Kandic and witness Krsto Djurovic, witness Handzijev and Djurovic. In view of this conclusion reached by the court with respect to the fact that there is no proof that witness Mile Kandic ordered the accused to mobilise units, it is clear that the court -- well, it goes on to talk about the description, et cetera, et cetera. What is important is that at the end of it, the very serious charge of subverting the JNA was not sustained because the evidence was not there. Now, if Krsto Djurovic issued an order the next day, which apparently was the next day, not the same day, as you suggested, disobeying an order of Djurovic was punished. But there was never, according to the court that you respect, an order by Kandic, and Kandic himself had the opportunity to come to court and say it didn't happen. Did you ever apologise to Milisic for what you said or did?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object to this course of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If my learned colleague, and of course she has the right to bring into question the witness's credibility if she wishes to impeach him by indicating the differences between what he said here in Court or what he said before the military court, then the proper course, as I understand it, would be to present him with his witness statement, the one he gave before the military court. But doing it this way, to challenge this by juxtaposing the conclusions of a trial chamber which had evidence and exhibits before them - who knows which kind - with what the witness ought to have said or might have said, is quite inappropriate. So if we have the transcript of this witness, then I think he ought to be shown the transcript and that the examination should be conducted on the basis of that transcript and his statements, and then the Trial Chamber can draw their conclusions on the basis of all those facts. Whereas if we just hear the judgement and we don't know the reasons stated, I don't think we can continue in this way. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. There would normally be much in what you say, but in this case the witness has had no difficulty saying what evidence he did give and that the charge, or one of the charges, the critical charge, was based upon that evidence. And we will no doubt receive a copy of the decision of the court, but it has been read to the witness, in which it is clear that the person whom the witness said gave the order, gave evidence to the court that he did not give that order in that conversation, and the court therefore accepted that evidence and preferred that over the evidence of the present witness. Surely all that has been established without controversy or uncertainty. Just what, if anything, this Tribunal might make of that is yet a different question. But the basic facts appear in this case to be not disputed, and therefore, what has occurred is one to which I think no valid objection can be made, subject, of course, to us receiving the actual authenticated decision at an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever offer an apology to Captain Milisic?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, may I be allowed to explain? Since you've been doing so much reading --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... apology?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please might the witness be allowed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have asked me a great number of things. Now, you give me a chance to explain and listen to me for a change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you would just listen to the questions put to you and answer those questions. A little later, you can be asked again about this by the other counsel, and if you have further explanations that you want to give, you will be able to give them. So don't be disturbed that you are being gagged and precluded from giving your view. But it will be up to counsel for the Defence whether it wants to pursue the matter further with you. Now, if you would listen to the questions being put to you and try and answer those questions and not anything else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever offer an apology to Captain Milisic?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm happy to have you ask that question. I did not offer an apology, but, you see, there's always some justice, and the truth and justice will win out. A month ago, or perhaps two months ago, my wife's cousin from Kula came to Split. He's in Pula. He came to Tivat, actually, and he came to see us, not to me personally, but -- because I live with a cousin of mine. So he was there accommodated for three days, living with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... want to talk about matters. My question was: Did you ever offer an apology to Captain Milisic? It is a very simple question. A yes or a no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the answer has been given. No. If you want to explore it further with questions, do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If not, move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever --

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please may I be allowed to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... question, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be up to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Your Honours, the first thing I'm going to say is important. Milisic sent greetings via this man and said, "Veso, tell Pere that I'm not angry at him at all." The man is alive, so you can ask him. And he said to him, "Pere, I'm not angry with him at all." So that answers you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I'm glad you've managed to get that off your chest.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Handzijev.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm even more thankful for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you were asked about subordination to the military naval district. I would ask the usher, please, to show D44, please, if I may. The exhibit before you is an exhibit that the Defence has offered to this Court, and I would ask you to take a look at the information in it and particularly turn your attention to page 2 in your language, or in -- maybe it's not in your language, in B/C/S. Page 2, point D.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it, yes. I didn't think I had it, but I've found it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please be good enough to read that out loud, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean B?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I mean D, as in Don.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, D. I see it, right. The 9th VPS with the 4th Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade will use land forces in coordinated action with the Titograd TO Brigade to defeat enemy forces and take control of Prevlaka and will use sea forces to control entry to the Bay of Kotor. It will prevent the enemy from manoeuvring or operating and will provide naval artillery support to land forces and is to be in a state of readiness to conduct a seaborne landing if the need arises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you look at the very end of this document and indicate, please, whose signature is on that, where it comes from, what formation it comes from.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd Operational Group, Lieutenant Colonel General Jevrem Cokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever had dealings with Colonel General Cokic? Did you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I had any dealings with him. I remember him. But I don't remember having had any dealings with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what happened to Captain Djurisic -- Djurovic, excuse me. I beg your pardon. Djurovic.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: When warship Captain Djurovic was hit, the helicopter, at that time I was near the area. I was around the village of Komi [as interpreted] on the road to Cilipi, and I was there with the chief of artillery and another man, a reservist. That's where we were. I was free, so I decided to go and take a look at what was happening over there, the situation over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you come to learn about -- when you say I decided to take a look at what was happening over there, were you referring to the incident with the helicopter?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at that position before the helicopter arrived. We saw the helicopter when it was flying towards the Konavle ridge. That's the name of the area. And we saw him make a circle, and suddenly we couldn't hear the sound of the helicopter any more. He went round Cilipi and returned to the village of Komaja where there was operations going on. Suddenly we didn't hear any noise, any -- the noise of the helicopter, and later we learnt that the helicopter had been hit and that Cokic was in it, it appeared, and that the helicopter was hit and that that's when our commander was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you knew of Colonel General Cokic. You knew that he was in the helicopter, you knew that he was a player in theatre? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. But I learnt later on that he offered Captain -- warship Captain Djurovic to go with him, but I didn't know while he was actually flying. We didn't know who was in the helicopter when it was up in the area. This is something that we learnt later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you familiarised yourself, as an operations officer, had you familiarised yourself with this document which is labelled D44 at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. Maybe I saw it, maybe I didn't see it. These are not my documents. These are documents of the command. I don't remember. These are documents that higher authorities, higher commands, handle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you would be good enough to show P119 and P121, please. I think if we look at the document, dated the - let's see - 24th -- 23rd of October. I think that's P121, if I am not wrong. I'm sorry. P119 is dated 24th of October. And if you look at -- well, we've got two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at P121. I know it's funny that they have opposite higher numbers. But P121 first and then P119. Mr. Handzijev, do you have in front of you P121, which is an order dated 23rd of October, 1991? It is addressed to the command of the 9th VPS and the 472nd Motorised Brigade. Do you see that? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it just fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's a -- it's basically a combat order. And whose signature or whose name is at the bottom of the order, if you can see, please?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major General Pavle Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you familiarise yourself at the time with this order? Were you at Kumbor during this time, 23 October 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Kumbor. But as for this document, I'm not the person to whom this document is submitted. It can be seen very nicely here. I am the operations centre, so such orders are not given to me. There's no need to give them to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are an operations centre officer; is that right? You were at the time. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you indicating to us that one of your functions is not the transmittal of orders and other vital information from the theatre of combat?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is transmitted to my superior. And now the superior does familiarise us with certain things, as he deems necessary. But the service that I performed in peacetime, as a duty-officer, well, that's a different question altogether. I have my immediate superior officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the 23rd of October the activity discussed is not activity of peacetime. Are you saying you did not familiarise yourself with this particular -- the content of this document and/or this document?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please, Madam Usher, show P, I believe it is 119, which is the second document, dated 24 October. Now, this document is addressed -- it is from the command of the 2nd Operational Group, addressed to the 2nd Corps, the 37th Corps, the 9th VPS, and the 472nd Motorised Brigade. It's a decision for further action. And could you tell us, please: At the end of the document under -- whose name appears at the end of the document?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, General Pavle Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time - the time being 24 October 1991 - had you familiarised yourself with this document that was addressed to your formation, the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were asked a question by counsel referring to a matter in the war diary, which is D96, the war diary for Kupari. I would like to ask you, though: Where is the war diary, or the log, which you indicate was required to have been kept, for your operations centre?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not quite understand. Where it was or where it is now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... now?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I've been a pensioner since 2000. It has to be in archives. This is a lasting document. It has to be in the archives of the 9th VPS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you became aware that you would be giving evidence before this Tribunal, did you attempt to familiarise yourself with the events over which you would have responsibility for documenting by seeking the log for your formation? I'm sorry. For your operations centre. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed that this logbook went missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who informed you of that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: My judge, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And went missing. Where should it have been that it went missing? What were you told about that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I was made this offer to testify, the first thing that crossed my mind was that logbook, because everything is regulated in that logbook, everything is written in that logbook. So every order, every contact, the main things that happened. So the first thing that crossed my mind was the logbook. As a matter of fact, when Mr. Rodic and I talked, he said, "No problem. I'll go to the archives to look for the logbook." Or rather, I said that I would go to the archives to look this up in the logbook, and he said, "Don't bother. It's not there."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try to go anyway?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. I didn't. I mean, I believed him. To tell you the truth, I didn't have the time to either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was it that you were invited to testify? I'm sorry. I think you said, "When I was made this offer to testify," on page 27, line 5. When was that offer to testify made?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just let me think. I don't know exactly. Mr. Rodic will know. Was it 15 or 20 days before I came here? I think, around that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, without giving details, I don't want to intrude on your privacy, but could you tell us what city you live in now and what republic where you're currently residing, just generally. Not street or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I live in the small town of Tivat, in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Kumbor, where your command post was during the time that we're discussing, in which republic is Kumbor?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in which republic is Kupari?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in which republic is Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is part of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most probably. I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you describe for us, please: Did you work in shifts in the operations centre? Give us an idea of what your -- how your work logistically was. Did you work shifts? Were they regular? Were they day, night, alternated? Help us out with that, please.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we worked in shifts, for the most part. That's right. For example, I would be there until 1.00 as the operations officer, the professional. So there were mainly people coming from the rear or from the command, and then there was this list of duty officers, and they were sort of assistants and they were there from midnight until the morning. That's how they were on duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your duty shift 5 December 1991? What shift did you work on the 5th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I was on duty on the 5th of December or whether I was on duty on the 6th of December, I think. In view of the war logbook, Kozaric told me to look for Colonel Kovacevic, so that's probably when I was on duty. And if the war logbook were here, I would have certainly been able to find this, when I was on duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your only recollection of anything about the 6th would have been what was in the war logbook?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that document would be sufficient to remind me that I was working on that day. But that doesn't matter, because as duty-officer at the operations centre, it was my duty to be present at the centre every day. And actually, this duty was only formally in shifts. We were supposed to work together, not even two people were sufficient. We would get reinforcements. We had two men there in addition. So it doesn't matter whether I was on duty or not. I was there non-stop practically. Only sometimes I'd go out on a particular task or whatever, but ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the 5th of December, were you in the operations room, hearing transmissions, receiving telephone calls, doing what operations officers are known to do?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said that we were permanently there and that we complemented each other. And it was in this entire period. There were four professionals, four of us were professionals. And I said very nicely yesterday: We had a hundred tasks, and I was personally sought by the mothers, because I was well known throughout the former Yugoslavia. They were looking for me personally because I was the most persistent person in this respect. I was looking for their sons, and I was trying to establish telephone contact for them. So I don't know how the word spread, but they were looking for me personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 5th of December, what calls, what messages, what information did you take down, receive, and transmit? Can you tell us that, please?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. You just have to remind me with something. I can't really say anything just off the cuff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about on the 4th of December? What information, messages, phone calls did you receive?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember now. But if you were to show me a document, perhaps it would remind me. Of course I received messages. We received different messages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 7th of December, 1991, what messages, phone calls, information did you receive and transmit?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean specifically? Well, different information, different messages. A hundred telephone calls a day. I can't remember exactly what you mean -- I mean what you're interested in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in the Dubrovnik area on the 6th of December? Tell us your understanding of what happened, please.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my prism. First of all, you've reminded me just now when you said what happened. I know what happened. There were preparations for negotiations. I personally, as a human being, was most pleased. I mean, I'd been wearing boots for a year, wouldn't take them off. So when I heard about this, I mean I remember these messages that this boat was supposed to come from Split, or rather, this minister was supposed to come for these negotiations in Cavtat. So I was really pleased about that. But then on the 6th, on the 6th I was really surprised, I mean surprised. This optimism of mine became pessimism. The negotiations were gladly expected. But what happened, happened. There were people dead, dead on both sides, in fact. And as I said yesterday, I listened to a conversation. I don't know who Rudolf was talking to. He probably used Radio Dubrovnik, Radio Bar, that connection, communication line, and then our operations centre. I wasn't there, but I did -- when I came in, I realised that something was happening, and I know that Rudolf was in a panic and he was saying that that whole old nucleus was on fire. There's general panic. There are people dead. And I was surprised. We were just caught out. So perhaps that's what you referred to. This was from 9.00 onwards. I don't know the exact time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you.: You said the whole old nucleus was on fire. What were you referring to, or what was he referring to, as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Old Town. That's what I understood him to mean. And sometimes this was used for propaganda purposes, this whole sort of panic. So I wasn't sure whether it was propaganda or whether it was true, whether it was true or not. Now, if something is really on fire, you can't hide that, and of course the European Mission was there and the observers were there observing. So quite simply, to be quite frank, I expected peace and I became very pessimistic because I wasn't expecting war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That 6th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just told us that sometimes this was used for propaganda purposes, this whole sort of panic. Now, when a call comes in to you which tells you that the Old Town of Dubrovnik is on fire, whether you subjectively believe it is true or not, what do you do about it? I mean, just in case it's true, what do you do about it? What is your course of action?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that was not the witness's statement, that he was called, as we all remember. He listened to the conversation between Rudolf and someone else. He's not the one who was called by Rudolf. So could the witness's evidence please be followed carefully.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Shall I rephrase it to say that the conversation on which you eavesdropped, in which you gained information that the Old Town of Dubrovnik was on fire, now, what did you do about it? Did you pretend not to hear the conversation because you were eavesdropping or did you decide that you should take some action? Tell us what you did about it.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this part of the conversation, I think it was the end of the conversation. I cannot tell you exactly whether he talked to Jokic or Jeremic, because Jeremic was liaison officer on our side with the European Mission. And at any rate, all these protests went through Jeremic. I cannot say anything for sure now. I don't know whether at that moment I was at the operations centre listening to something else, but I walked in and I heard Rudolf panic-stricken. I didn't even know it was Rudolf, you see. It was only later that my assistant who was there who had turned this on -- I mean, he's the one who establishes this communication. I mean, it's only later that I found out that this was Rudolf. I heard that there was a fire, that there were dead people. And then there is the five-pointed star up there, soldiers, barrels pointing at town. That's what I heard. And now what did I do? I mean, as a professional soldier, first I have to see whether it is correct, whether it is propaganda. But later on, when I found out that there were some actions taking place there and that the members of the ZNG were firing from Dubrovnik, that is the information I received, that they were opening mortar fire and this -- these -- with the PAM guns, 20-, 30-millimetres, and they were firing at our forces that were on Srdj. We were nearby. I mean --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do about it?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: What could I do about it? I mean, I'm not somebody who can do something about it. I mean, in the meantime -- actually, I don't know how much time had elapsed, but then Kadijevic called. I don't know if it was an hour later or whatever. But at any rate, it was all up to midday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me for cutting you off. Did you, as the operations officer on duty, did you inform your superiors of the content of the call which you had overheard about what Mr. Rudolf said was happening in Dubrovnik? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I -- well, this was just a transit conversation, this conversation about the cease-fire. I mean, who could I tell about this? Our command had probably received this already. It can only be sent to them. So then if Rudolf went -- well, I can't remember now who it was, I mean who this assistant of mine was. It was Radio Dubrovnik, Radio Bar. And Radio Bar, in our case --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you inform your superiors about the content of the call that you were listening to, to the effect that Dubrovnik was on fire? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: My superiors were all at the forward command post, so we were just transit. This was transit communication. And my superior officers were probably already listening to all of this there at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you confirm with the forward command post that your superior officers were indeed there? Did you do what you were supposed to do and confirm that and transit the information?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I heard this, but he had already been put through, and they listened to that. My superiors heard that. And at that moment, we found out that there was fighting there at Srdj, that our people were up there, Zec and the commander, that they were all in the area and there's nothing for us to confirm. I mean, we're there just to transit to the command -- I mean, unless we were given a direct order to convey something to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the missing log from your operations centre should ever surface, will we find an entry in there by you as to this conversation that you overheard by a man who was identified to you, you say later, as Mr. Rudolf, about Dubrovnik and the Old Town being on fire? Will we find that entry there?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, I'm not sure. I mean I cannot say anything with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, would this be a convenient time for a break? I'd like to get my voice back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it certainly would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Handzijev, you had told us just before the break in response to my question about: Did you confirm with the forward command post that your superior officers were indeed there? You said: "My superiors heard that. And at that moment, we found out that there was fighting there at Srdj, that our people were up there, Zec and the commander, that they were all in the area, and there's nothing for us to confirm. I mean, we're just there to transit to the command." Now, Zec and the commander. Whom did you mean? Zec we know. Which commander were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the commander who was there at the forward command post of the 9th VPS, the forces that were engaged in fighting. That was Admiral Jokic. Jokic and Zec were there, and we had been informed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Perhaps I'm misunderstanding you. Jokic was where? Where was Jokic?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jokic, according to my information, was in the area now, the forward command post or in Cavtat. I don't know. But he was in the area. Right now, I can't remember his exact whereabouts at the time. That area was always the same thing for me, the forward command post, Cavtat. He was somewhere in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you are aware, then, at this point, from what we're seeing as of the time of this message coming in, that there is combat going on, that units of the 9th VPS are involved, and that when you refer to fighting at Srdj, then these units are involved in that fighting. Do we understand each other on that point?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that Srdj had some fighting on it. You said: "My superiors heard that, and at the moment we found out there was fighting there at Srdj, that our people were up there, Zec and the commander." So we understand each other in that some officers who were -- some persons who were part of the 9th VPS were at Srdj, and -- as you understand it, and that there was combat activity going on? Can we start from that point? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not quite right. I didn't say that the officer had gone to Srdj or anywhere. I didn't know where they were, whether on Srdj -- I didn't know where they were. I knew that they were in the area, but I didn't know exactly where the commander Admiral Jokic, Admiral Zec. I'm not sure where they were, the forward command post or somewhere near, maybe en route. We simply didn't have that kind of information. I'm not sure if you understand me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to try. Now, who is Gavro Kovacevic, Colonel Gavro Kovacevic? Do you know who that was, is?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gavro Kovacevic was the assistant commander for the land forces or for the infantry. He is a colonel by rank, and he was supposed to be also at the forward command post at that point in time. So according to the dispatch that I received, I was supposed to call him, but he was not present there, and his presence was needed, because they were looking for him urgently. Probably something to do with the equipment. I'm not sure why they were looking for him, but most probably that was the reason, and most probably we eventually found him. I just can't remember whether we did or not. We probably found him. But since it was urgent and since he was needed, we probably found him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now what. Many now, the order -- I'm sorry, but the transmission you referred to, I guess, is the one that was read to you this morning on page 70 of the Kupari log, at 1349, where it says: Frigate Captain Handzijev was ordered to call Bileca and Trebinje and to immediately order Colonel Kovacevic to come to the IKM KVPS." Now, was it your understanding that if you were to call Bileca and Trebinje that -- to get Colonel Kovacevic, that he was in that area? Would that have been your understanding?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my understanding -- what you're asking me about, they knew approximately at the forward command post, they knew where Kovacevic was, since they ordered me to find him in Trebinje or Bileca. So they knew. He's their own man, and he worked with them at that command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, which command --

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: They knew at every single point in time Kovacevic's whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now what is in Trebinje, Bileca? Why would you be -- what would you communicate with in Trebinje and Bileca? Is there an operations centre there that you can tell us about?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know exactly what there was at Trebinje, there was the command of the 2nd Operational Group at Trebinje. Now, as for Bileca, I can't quite remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you remember, once you got this -- if your memory is jogged and you say this is what refreshes your memory on this, when you got this order, did you call the command post or the command operations centre at the command post at the 2nd Operational Group to track down Colonel Kovacevic and indicate that he was to come to the forward command post at Kupari?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally don't remember this bit of information, because this very task is a task that I charged my assistant with. I may have left later on. I may have been absent from there. But for me, this order is a minor one. Therefore, I did not attach great importance to it. Our assistant probably sent it on or informed someone. But we had a direct communication line with Trebinje. It would have been enough for me to press a button for the protected channel or for the open channel, public channel. It was a direct link. If you want me to, I'll explain exactly how this worked, this line of communication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why don't you tell us how you communicated directly with the 2nd --

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translations continues]... that switchboard that we had, for example, it was like a small switchboard for communications. We had over ten direct links on two channels; a protected channel and an ordinary channel. Now, on that line, we had first the General Staff, the cabinet, the direct line and the ordinary line. We had the operations centre of the General Staff also on both lines. Then we also had the navy administration also on both lines. We had the main units. And as for civilian bodies, we had the air traffic control at Tivat. We had Radio Bar, a direct link. They had to call us. We had frequent communications from the Main Staff, incoming communications, over the radio, and Radio Bar they only had to press a button and they would engage us. And then I had a line with the commander, with Jokic, a direct link. That's as far as the commands are concerned. I had one with the forward command post, a direct link, both protected and open. And this worked well. I could have put anyone through to anyone else. And then there was a civilian number, and they could have called me while I was manning the switchboard, and I could have held conference calls with all these participants. I'm not sure if you get my meaning. So it was like a small switchboard that we had there. I just needed to press a button for the 2nd Operational Group and I would have been put through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you -- on a regular basis push that button for the 2nd Operational Group and keep them informed of matters that were relevant, matters that should go to their attention? I would assume you would have done that as a good operations officer wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know something. When there was something important for them, yes, we would do that. But it was only rarely that my operational centre got in touch with them. There was no need for us to get in touch with them. Perhaps on a couple of occasions. That was perhaps some information that was relevant to them. Not that operational centre, but with my forward command post, we had a line that was open almost all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you would be able, from what I understand, with this sophisticated switchboard you described, you would be able to communicate matters that you thought were important and that you should pass up to Kupari and the 2nd Operational Group and pretty much -- and Main Staff? I mean, you had direct access to all. Now, let me ask -- did I understand you correctly on that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't -- let me tell you. We were not a relevant factor in terms of conveying information. We were some sort of transit, transit, you understand. If there was information travelling through our transit, it was like registering things in the logbook. It was some sort of a transit. I would just convey these things. And the end user would then make entries in their own logbook. We were just transit. We were switchboard and people were conveying hundreds and thousands of calls and messages through us, individuals, in terms of providing security for materiel, in terms of relocation. We would just put people through to one another and then information itself would travel on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in terms of information you might consider important, if, for example, I mean, God forbid, but let's say Admiral Jokic had been in an auto accident or something and someone contacted your command post that they needed to get an emergency vehicle to render assistance, would you pass that information on to the relevant superior commands? Would you deem that important information, if a commander of your unit -- I mean, I'm giving you an example, but just as a type of information that might get passed up.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd forward it to the VPO and then on to the General Staff. If there's something that happens to a commander, then you would need to inform the operations centre of the General Staff and the VPO, because that was our first superior command. But we also informed the General Staff about these things, or the forward command post. If they had not been informed, then they, in their own report -- because we were not the ones writing the report. They were the ones writing the report to the command. And we were some sort of supplement there, in a manner of speaking. We were more into peacetime affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we accept that there were combat activities going on in the area of Srdj and that the order to you was to get Captain -- I'm sorry, Colonel Kovacevic back to the forward command post at Kupari, did you link -- sorry. Did you view returning -- I'm sorry. Let me rephrase that. I want to make sure I don't give you the wrong question. Captain -- Colonel Kovacevic was, to your knowledge, also involved that day in the activities that were taking place up on Srdj? Do you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. I didn't know about those operations at all. I found out by accident after I'd heard that conversation. And then, after that, when the chief of General Staff called. It was only then that I found out, at 10.00 or 11.00, I found out that something had been going on over there. It was only then that I found out about those operations, that one of our units had moved on Srdj. That was the information, and I put two and two together. And then later you do find out, because you know we had people coming to the forward command post and people talk. They exchange information. But it's been many years since and I'm not sure exactly how it happened, but we did know that there had been casualties in town and up there also, and that things were on fire. It was no secret.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... said came from the chief of the General Staff. You said it was around 10.00 or 11.00. You give it that time frame. Can you be -- can you commit to that time frame?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I didn't say I said -- before midday. I'm not sure in terms of time. I can't be very resolute about this. The time period -- there were so many things happening. At that time I really can't give you the exact time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... ever surfaces, are we going to find an entry in the logbook by you about a phone call like this?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may be one there, but maybe not. It was also a transit call. I'm not saying anything. There may be something. But, for example, if the chief of General Staff had called Jokic, this was a possibility, but it doesn't mean that it necessarily happened. It was just transit. When I received the call from that first person, I wasn't there at the time. I mean, I was around there, but when the General Staff calls, apart from the sound signal, you have a light beaming and it shows exactly who's calling. And when the General Staff is calling, then the most senior person answers the call. I jumped up immediately. I pressed a button. And there you have it. I answered the call.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... did you jump up because it was an important person you believed to be on the other end of the line?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as soon as it's the General Staff and not the operations centre, it means someone from the General Staff, and the General Staff, well, the person who most often called was Admiral Brovet. He called quite often. Sometimes he even called about some things -- some things that should be conveyed or perhaps warnings that he had for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you is: Did you jump up when you saw the light because it was an important person on the other end of the line?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I think I can't remember exactly how it was. But I know that, for example, someone said: General Staff on the line. The assistant who is there or perhaps talking elsewhere to someone. There are several lines of communication next to the switchboard. There are two telephones. So all in all, I know -- well, I don't know exactly how it was. It wasn't yesterday, after all. But I know that when the General Staff calls, all in all, I personally picked up the phone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or answered that call. That much is certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A call from the General Staff -- you described, for example, the order to go and find Colonel Kovacevic as minor, in your eyes. That minor point made it into -- that minor point, as you see from the papers in front of you, did make it into the logbook for Kupari. Were you able, in reviewing -- did you review this logbook in its entirety, this Kupari section that was -- you've been asked about? Did you review it?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I reviewed it in relation to the dates about the 6th. But as for anything else -- that order, you know, it must be written down. But this is just transit. You know what I mean when I say "transit." The person who -- over there who -- well, they can write it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, a minor -- something that's minor, in your eyes, such as getting Colonel Kovacevic, made it into the book. I looked for -- through the 6th, and perhaps I missed it, but could you take a look for us and find out if a call from General Staff looking for Admiral Jokic made it into this logbook. Could you just take a quick look, if you don't mind. If you could find that entry for me, I'd be grateful. I might have missed it.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No what? I'm sorry. No what? Are you willing to --

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I mean, this call, you mean in their logbook, whether it was recorded there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Right. Did you see -- if you would maybe take a quick look.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it's not in that logbook. When I looked at it, the logbook from the forward command post, I mean. But that doesn't necessarily mean that they ... What am I supposed to do now? What am I supposed to go through?
