utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could take a look, please, for the entries on the 6th of December, and if you could find an entry that indicates that General Kadijevic was looking for Admiral Jokic through Kumbor and that there was a call. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, this logbook has nothing to do with that. That call, that was through us. And now, where I found Jokic, one number or other, I can't remember which phone number I used. But that's not really that important. The important thing is: At the time there was a conversation with the content that I told you about. I am prepared to swear that what I'm telling you is the truth. This conversation did take place at that time, and the content of that conversation that I gave you faithfully reflects the conversation. Maybe Jokic himself will remember, if he's willing to remember the conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe you can help us. Yesterday you indicated that you called Kupari searching for Admiral Jokic. Do you find in that Kupari logbook that you have in front of you that -- any reference to your search for Admiral Jokic? After all, he is your commander.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not in the logbook, but if I said that I asked for Kupari, the normal procedure, the principal, Jokic was certainly not the commander. If he had been the commander to ours, he would have had a direct link or communication to the General Staff there, for General Kadijevic would not have needed to call him or to call me or that man over there. Therefore, he would have phoned directly. Now as to where I found Jokic, I can't remember, but the crux of the matter is, we had hundreds of conversations. I called Jokic very many times a day. I would put him through, you know, when I found him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry for interrupting, but what we see on page 45, between line 8 and line 16, I can't intervene for the transcript itself, but when the tape is reviewed, can this please be checked. Because what was actually said does not correspond with what has been written down. So therefore, when the transcript is checked, can the extra attention please be paid to this section of the witness's testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. That request has been noted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate to us whether or not you know about the connections that exist from Cavtat to Dubrovnik? What do you know about the connections, communications connections from Cavtat to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: So Cavtat-Dubrovnik. I knew about that. There was a line, they had one line from Dubrovnik, like I said, through Radio Dubrovnik. And this was the more commonly used line. And there was another line between Dubrovnik and the command at Mokosica, the local command. You could establish communication. And the local command, well, it could -- well, but sometimes the line was busy. Sometimes it was too busy or the line was down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I just want to check the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit, if you're familiar with the process, about faxes. Did you receive and send faxes in the course of your work as an operations officer in Kumbor?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Through our encryption officer we were able to send faxes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us the distance between Cavtat and Kupari?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cavtat, Kupar [as interpreted], I have no idea how many kilometres. I don't think I could say. Certainly not more than five kilometres, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They're pretty close to each other?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not far.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they're both in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Both in Croatia, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, they had direct telephone communication, given their closeness to each other, right, those two locations?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes, but I don't know exactly. I can't say. Well, probably they did have. Logically speaking, they should have had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. When you took a look at the Kupari war diary, or the log - I'd really rather call it just the communications log - what was it that you were looking for? What particular entries were you looking for, before you came to the courtroom to testify, you know, whatever time you arrived in The Hague and had a chance to review this?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing specific, truth to tell. I wasn't looking for anything specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could -- do you have the document in front of you? If you would be good enough to look at page 66, please. Have you found the page? If you could look at the entry for 2155 hours.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. 2155 hours. It says: "Radio surveillance. Ammunition has arrived in Stun [phoen] as well as another thing is and going for Dubrovnik. Frigate Captain Handzijev." Now, tell us about the radio surveillance. What this means, what was your role in this transmission. What is this all about?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's for purposes of monitoring.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were you monitoring?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just go through it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what this information has to do with radio surveillance now. The question is about radio surveillance, what they did. Of course, they were eavesdropping. I'm not sure at all what this information has to do with anything. It was conveyed to me. I was the operational centre, after all, and this is something that I should keep in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you involved, then, in interceptions of radio communications? When you say "eavesdropping," were you talking about listening to communications of the other --

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And what did you do with that information that you got? What did you -- if you found information that would have an impact on the course of your -- of the units that were in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Operational Group or the 9th VPS together, what would you do? I'm sorry. And the 9th VPS. Right.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This sort of information, if it was really important, we would convey this sort of information to our forward command post. We would convey it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who decided if it was really important?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who decided? I decided, for example, if I was on duty on a specific day. If it was someone else, then the other person made the decision, depending who was on duty on a particular day. But it was our service, our unit that decided, depending on the degree of importance of a certain bit of information. There were different kinds of information, but mostly we conveyed all of the information that we received. I'm not sure what the meaning is behind this, but that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so, as information or intelligence came in through interception, part of your function, as I just understood what you said, was to assess that intelligence and pass it on or not pass it on, as you deemed appropriate?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how important a question this is, but we passed on almost all the information, and that's why we were, as I said, some sort of a transit station. All the information we couldn't relay directly -- they couldn't relay directly to them. They could only have gone through us, and that's what we did. I was not the one to say how important it was, but it could have been an innocuous piece of information, and it was a subjective call for us whether we would pass it on or not. Something really innocuous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in intercepting communications from the other side, which have potentially intelligence value, then you, as an operations officer, also had, as part of your duties, some intelligence function as well, from what you've just described, or did I get it wrong?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you got it wrong. As I said, our role was surveillance, monitoring the situation in our area of responsibility, on the ground, in the air, and also information was part of that. There were war operations afoot. It doesn't matter how you obtain information, whether it's radio surveillance, radar surveillance, but we got the information and we passed it on, sure thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you in the early morning hours of the 6th of December, please? Tell us exactly where you were.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Perhaps I was at the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which command?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the 9th VPS. And my area, my area of movement, was the operations centre, perhaps my office, the canteen, the toilet, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say command of the 9th VPS, are you referring to Kumbor or are you referring to --

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Kumbor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, didn't you have several communications from Captain Slobodan Kozaric in the early morning hours of the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could judge from the diary, I was not. I don't remember. But from what I saw in the diary, all I can do is look through it again perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't remember? You don't remember it?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So your recollection about activities in the early morning of the 6th of December would be only what you could glean from or take from any possible entries in the war diary. Is that what you're trying to tell me, tell the Chamber? You don't have an independent recall of that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall. It's like this: You know, some things you remember a long time. Other things you forget very quickly. And it's been 12 years since that time. So depending on the weight of the information and the events and all that kind of thing. Some things in the space of 12 years, even a computer, the virus hits the computer and the information is lost. So ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now -- excuse me. I'm sorry. In other words, what you're saying is a lot of things occur and you don't have the ability to recall everything. Now, how can you -- how are you --

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that a call that may have come from General Kadijevic came on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Kadijevic did not call very often, and he did not call unless he had some major reason. We were at peace for a long time, and the most important event that happened was that if it was an important event, he would have to intervene personally, and that was the event. That was the most important event, the major event. So after a long period of time, this happened, those operations happened. And that was the period of time and that particular event when Kadijevic got involved personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what operations are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the movement of forces towards Srdj. That's what I mean, general movement, unnecessary commotion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you --

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only a madman --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. I apologise. Were you also at the operations centre of -- at Kumbor between the 23rd and the 25th of October, 1991, and the 8th and the 13th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. But could you give me an event to jog my memory? What events are you referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues].. give me an event to jog your memory. You mentioned operations. I mean, are you aware of any operations that took place affecting the 2nd Operational Group or the area around Dubrovnik or the 9th VPS during those periods of time?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I do know about one particular operation, and I'll describe it, if you want me to, and explain. This is how it was: It was the landing at Kupari. The landing at Kupari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did that take place? Tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the date. I really can't give you a date. But I do remember the event well, but I don't remember the date when it took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you something. As a result of that landing at Kupari -- up to that time, had the 9th VPS OPS centre been exclusively at Kumbor?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was it?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was out there. When the landing took place, afterwards, maybe one hour later after the landing, we had General Strugar on the line, Pavle Strugar, when the landing took place, and he asked to speak to Jokic, Admiral Jokic. And Jokic came to the phone - and I'm quoting now - did he say, "Mijo, what are you doing? That's not a good thing. What you're doing is not a good thing. Do you know where my forces are?" And he wanted to answer, or maybe he did say something, but he said, "Don't tell me anything now. I'll come and see you." So when I heard this, I was -- felt unrest, because I felt there was no subordination between Strugar, General Strugar, the commander of the 2nd Operational Group, and Jokic. And I came to realise Jokic was working on his own, on his own bat, that the landing had been done that way. I remember that very well. But I can't give you a date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, okay. Now, how do you remember this so clearly -- how do you remember those words so clearly after all those years?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said: Some things remain deep in your memory. Other things don't. And that's how my brain works, at least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after this landing at Kupari, did anything change in terms of the location of the communications centre? At what point did there become an operations centre, the IKM? When did that take place?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably after that. I can't remember. I didn't pay attention to it. I know that one of our groups went. We divided up. So probably after that, as soon as Kupari was taken, then quite naturally they would go to the command post. That would be quite normal. The front is moved forwards, and that is why it's called the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the words that you said, I won't read the whole thing, but Mijo something, something, something by General Strugar, whatever you said. Why did these words -- maybe you can help us understand why these words led you to conclude anything on the issue of subordination? Whatever would have made you think about that in recalling those words that you've just told us today in 2004?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this. I have to say again, some things I remember well, others not. Sometimes I remember the tone of voice, for example, that was used when a word was uttered. I just understood and came to realise that General Strugar was caught unawares, and he was surprised at what this man was doing over there. And I said that I was between the hammer and the anvil, a rock and a hard place. I expected peace, and I thought that this subordination went from the General Staff downwards and that it was a stable chain of command. That's what I felt intimately. And suddenly I see that Jokic was taking over, taking some action, and the man who, for me, was his superior, that is to say, General Strugar, didn't know about it. So this is subordination or insubordination. And a quite unnatural set of events took place. So he worked on his own, on his own bat. He was launching an operation that he didn't have orders for. And there was an order from -- if there was an order for a landing, then the order should have come from General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that worry you? Did that concern you up to this day, this act? Have you been concerned about that up until now?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Today, today. What can we do today? I've been cooking in the Balkan cauldron for 63 years. So to take on all that responsibility for a landing on yourself, you know, a landing is a very complex operation. He didn't agree about it with him. You have to have coordination, conjoined forces, support forces, reinforcement from your neighbours. He was just taking it as if he was going to attend a wedding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me understand: That it was your understanding from the way you saw things then, from your perspective back then, and maybe perhaps up until this day, that you believe that General Strugar did not know that Kupari was going to be taken and that Admiral Jokic would be involved in that. Is that what your concern has been?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain that Strugar didn't know, and I'd cut off my head, I'd pledge that. Strugar certainly didn't know. Strugar was a knight, as far as I am concerned. And Dubrovnik ought to erect a monument to him to thank him for having Dubrovnik still stand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you view, as a result of this, Admiral Jokic as something less than a knight?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Correct. You put that very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what your feelings were, what it was that was troubling you about Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was troubling me about him. Well, I wanted everything to be solved in a peaceful way, that we should all go our ways without any casualties. And Jokic wasn't that kind of man. So for me personally, as far as I'm concerned, he was obsessed, to have his frustrations, the frustrations he experienced in Belgrade, where the mothers attacked him with their umbrellas in Belgrade, to go and do this kind of thing. So that was it. So as far as I was concerned, he was a renegade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't like Admiral Jokic, I take it.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: And another thing --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't like Admiral Jokic? I mean --

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can conclude that if you like. It's not that I've come here to testify against him, but he has no human qualities, no humaneness. And he's not a professional soldier. A professional soldier does not loot and plunder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me put your mind at rest. You seem to have been very concerned about an action in Kupari having occurred behind General Strugar's back, and you shouldn't leave here thinking that. If I could ask for a moment that P121, just for a moment, be put back on the ELMO. Do you have in front of you, Mr. Handzijev? I'm sorry. I'll wait.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No problem. If you will -- if you have the document in front of you, Mr. Handzijev. Can you look again -- you looked at it earlier today. It's dated 23rd of October. It's a signed for -- or it's under the signature of Major General Pavle Strugar and it goes to the 9th VPS. It is a combat order. And if you look at the very first paragraph, it does command the 9th VPS to take sections, including Kupari. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your conclusion about what was transpiring then between General Strugar and Admiral Jokic was a conclusion that you came to without full information, and it was an erroneous conclusion. Would you have to agree to that, now that you know what really happened?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not clear whether the landing has anything to do with this order. I can't conclude that. Because it doesn't mention the landing here at all. And if it's an order, then in the order, it must stipulate "landing." Because that landing needs several days to prepare, and coordination. You have to have a coordination plan. And judging by this order, maybe this is a movement of forces. That would be normal. Tactical movement of forces of some kind. But it doesn't specify landing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... where it says: "You should take four sets of sections," and it describes them, okay, and one of them is Kupari and Cavtat. Do you see that? Just -- if you see it, just say yes. If you don't see it, say no.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Usher. We've finished with that document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that one function of the operations centre was to monitor air and surface situations. Was that a type of weather monitoring scheme or the objectives of which were to keep units informed of weather forecasts and wind factors and things like that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we would receive dispatches. But monitoring, it was done with radars, TISTINA [phoen] was the system. It was a computerised system linked to the radar, the Falcon radar, produced in -- manufactured in Sweden. And that's what we used to monitor the situation. It was automatic monitoring, and we had two other radars as well, Decca radars. And then the data processing was manual and you had the monitoring. But everything in the air was done by radar, radar monitoring and computer monitoring and processing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I understand you correctly, the system was in place to keep the units informed of the situation with weather, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Weather situation. The facilities. You look at the whole of the sea. We have our territorial waters. That whole area, and we look at the different features, how many have you got on the sea. That is the surface situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... is that right, is to keep you advised of that information? You had the information, it was part of your system, your very sophisticated system; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, on 6 December, learn of calls between Captain Slobodan Kozaric and Captain Vladimir Kovacevic in Brgat and then subsequently in Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. What -- Kovacevic? Captain Kovacevic? I don't know. I can't remember. I don't have it in my memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you become aware of calls between Captain Slobodan Kozaric and battleship Captain Chief of Staff Milan Zec on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. Perhaps I knew it at the time, but not now. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the -- other than the entry on page 70, did you become aware of calls between Captain Kozaric and Colonel Gavro Kovacevic on the 6th of December, other than the reference that may have been made? I'm asking you if you know of any other calls that may have been made between them on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Oh, at least I can't remember. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember calls between - on the 6th of December - Admiral Jokic and I believe it is Colonel Gojko Djurasic of Mokosica?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They might have had direct links, direct communication. So they didn't have to go through us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember or know of calls between Admiral Jokic in Kumbor and General Strugar on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't remember?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember anything about that call. I don't know how it went, what lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, did any calls or communications come from General Strugar through your operations centre, any communications or calls that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know. I don't remember at all. We had communications with some other command, but I don't remember this. And if it was, it was minor, negligible. I don't remember. It didn't stay with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would be about a minor point?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably. I can only assume that. Don't hold me to my word. As long as it wasn't a major event, I didn't remember it. I just delete, like you would with a computer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask you, Mr. Handzijev, to take a look at the log from Kupari, please. If you could open it up to page 73, please. Are you there yet? Tell me when.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look, if we can, at -- well, two entries. The first one is at 1922, and it is -- it's for Lieutenant General Strugar from Dubrovnik, and it says: "Rudolf. Because the fire is burning in the old centre of Dubrovnik and threatening with horrible consequences due to the lack of water, we ask that you enable the entry of ships with water-cannons whose purpose is to extinguish the fires, from Korcula, Ploce, into the old harbour of Dubrovnik. It is an urgent and necessary intervention. We expect your initial consent, after which we would precisely inform you of the type of ships and their time of arrival." And then it bears, "Minister Davorin Rudolf." The next entry is 1930, for the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff: "Lieutenant General Pavle Strugar gives his initial consent for the arrival of the ships, tugboats with water-cannons into the old harbour of Dubrovnik in order to extinguish the fires. Please inform us timely of the ships' number so as to ensure their unimpeded passage." And at the bottom of the message is "Lieutenant General Pavle Strugar." Did you not know about this communication on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'll explain it to you. I said that a possible line of communication between the Crisis Staff and the forward command post directly would be via Mokosica, the command of the place called Mokosica, and I think it was Colonel Gojkovic or something like that, whatever his name was, who was over there. It doesn't matter. But anyway, in answer to your question, not to lose our valuable time. That question will be answered by the next witness, because it's his handwriting, that he received directly, he received this call directly. So you can clear that matter up with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to the next witness about any of this -- of these entries in the logs? Did you have any discussions with the next witness about this, while he and you were in The Hague together, if you were together?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That witness, who will be coming in here, the next one, he worked at the forward command post, the IKM. So he was the duty-officer there. And you can ask him about all these matters, and he'll be able to tell you. Because they received it directly. I didn't. My operations centre didn't receive it directly. Had my operations centre -- let me explain. Had my operations centre received information like this from Radio Bar -- we did used to receive telegrams, dispatches of that kind. But had I received it, then I would be able to say I conveyed -- that it was conveyed to Handzijev, and Handzijev conveyed it further on up to Strugar. That's what would have been recorded, that would be the entry. But you can see here that it was with the forward command post directly, and if you ask the next witness he'll be able to explain it all to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you was: Did you talk to the person who is the next witness about your testimony, about the witness's testimony? Did you discuss the case at all together, if you saw each other?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course. I can't lie and say we didn't. It's human to talk. It's human to jog each other's memory. If I said we didn't, I would be lying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of any particularly important messages or communications from the 4th or the 5th of December, 1991 that might have indicated to you that something was going to take place on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 6th I knew that Rudolf would come, that he would have a meeting in Cavtat and that a peace agreement would be signed. And I, as a human being, I was happy about that. I didn't know anything else other than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally become aware of any communications or messages that came across the operations centre on the 4th or the 5th of December that would have told you that the action that you described at Srdj was going to take place? Did you personally know of anything on the 4th or the 5th of December about that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely nothing. All I knew was about the negotiations. He was a minister. He was coming to -- for negotiations. How could I know about any actions or operation over there? Only a madman could do something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry to hold you up. I just want to find something mentioned to you that you discussed yesterday. I think you -- in discussing what you said was a conversation from General Kadijevic -- I'll just find the reference. Yesterday, I've just -- transcript reference from what I'm able to take out of LiveNote was at 13:30:50, beginning there. Now, you said that Kadijevic asked Jokic, well, I don't know on what terms they were. What are you doing there? Down there? Now either in the singular or in the plural. Whatever would make you wonder whether or not General Kadijevic would have used the singular or the plural? I mean, did you make note in every entry that you make in your logbook the person on the other end of the line spoke in the singular or the plural? I mean, why does that stick in your mind, 13 years, 14 years later? What jogged -- why would you say that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I tell you, I don't know. I mean, quite simply, somehow -- they were in Belgrade, you see. Now, I assumed, and I think, that they were on two terms, you see. But that's not important. I mean, I told you what the meaning is. I guaranteed that, morally, legally, whatever. I'm not going to lie. I haven't come here to lie. I want the truth to be told. I want you to catch the truth. But in the Balkan triangle, you cannot catch the truth. It seems to elude everyone. Try to understand what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your native language?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, my mother tongue. My mother tongue is Greek, and then my second mother tongue was Macedonian. And then Bulgarian. I don't know what my mother tongue is. I told you, my childhood was during the civil war in Greece, and then I left Greece, came to Yugoslavia, and now this Yugoslavia was killed. Well, you know, mother tongue. So I'm a man without a country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so your concern about the use of the second person pronoun, whether it was singular or plural, in a language that was not your mother tongue, was really that much on your mind, up to today -- or yesterday, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you, it's not important. You know what, these people who are close, you see, and I thought that -- well, you know, he was a minister of defence, Jokic was, and this man was in the General Staff, Chief of Staff. And you know, these people become intimate. They become close. And I think that they spoke to each other on "ti" terms, that is to say, in the second person singular. That doesn't matter. But that's the meaning of these words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we find the missing logbook from Kumbor, are we going to have an entry in there saying General Kadijevic spoke to Jokic using "ti"? Would you have made a note of that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you won't find it. I told you -- how should I put this? It was quite simply transmission. It wasn't an order. I mean, it was even immoral for me to hear this conversation, to listen to it. I could have simply pressed a button and not listened. But General Kadijevic was the chief of General Staff and I was interested in the situation. And I couldn't be at peace. I simply had to listen. I had -- I wanted to see what he wanted and what this was all about. It was about me. It was about my family. Where we're going to be, are we going to go to Macedonia or not. I mean, I think you understand me. It's not moral, it's not what an officer should do, it's not right, but I did listen to part of the conversation. And I'm telling you which part this is, and if this helps you get to the truth, I'll be very happy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Handzijev, the truth is, there was no conversation during the morning between General Kadijevic and Admiral Jokic that you overheard or didn't overhear; it didn't take place; and that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's the kind of information you have, I'm telling you what I remember. I remember that conversation. If you have some other kind of information through some intelligence services of yours, that's debatable too, as far as I'm concerned. I told you, I have no reason to attack anyone. I have not come here to defend Strugar or to defend Jokic. I've come here so that you could grasp the truth. That's why I came here. I am sure that this conversation took place. I vouch that with my own head. I didn't dream of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reason why we -- if we ever find the missing logbook from Kumbor, the reason why we won't find an entry about this conversation is because it didn't take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sit down, please, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please confirm or deny what I've just asked you or said. The reason we won't find it is because it didn't take place; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm telling you, I mean I'm not claiming this. Maybe we did register it, maybe we did not. But I think that this was transmission, this was transmitting. So there was no need for me to write it in the logbook. I mean, well, whatever. I mean, if you called me to come here as a witness, I'm telling you what I remember, and now whether it was entered into a logbook or not, well, you know what, there can be administrative errors too. We did not write it down. We are not very tidy or punctual. I mean, not everybody was that pedantic. I don't know if you understand what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has finished its cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I didn't allow you to make an objection at that moment because it was a most critical point in the cross-examination. Is there something you now wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what my friend said in terms of her tone and the substance of what she said may imply some kind of involvement of General Strugar's Defence counsel in the matter of whether this document exists or not, and I would resolutely like to refute any kind of insinuation if that is what my learned friend wanted to do at that point in time, and that is what I wished to react to then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I can only say I didn't detect that, so I think we can leave that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Re-examination, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could the witness please be given P121. Re-examined by Mr. Rodic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Handzijev, did you have time to read this document?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please do that now. Are you reading --

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The order for further actions to the command of the 9th VPS of the 472nd Motorised Brigade of the 23rd of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel come closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, now that you've read this in general terms, in this decision related for further actions, is there any mention of the landing in Kupari as a military operation?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any order, in any order, when a landing is planned, then there has to be a separate paragraph about that, and then it says --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me: When you look at the first paragraph, the last sentence says: "You should take four sets of sections 1:25.000 of that region with you (Dubrovnik, Dubac, Kupari-Cavtat)." From these sections of maps, can any conclusion be drawn in terms of a landing on Kupari being ordered?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it cannot. These are regular sections that refer to this entire area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I no longer need this. In the first part of the cross-examination, my learned friend put certain questions to you in relation to Ivan Milisic, the former Chief of Staff of the 9th Military Naval Sector; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Several questions were put to you in relation to the court proceedings that took place before the military court in Nis, in relation to the indictment against Ivan Milisic.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the role that you specifically had in those court proceedings? Just tell me what role.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you testify in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those court proceedings, as a witness, did you tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, just be brief and answer my questions. Apart from your testimony in these proceedings, did you confront any other witnesses that were heard in those proceedings?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was confronted with Admiral Kandic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. On the basis of what?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he had stated that there were so many events that he did not remember that he ordered Ivo -- I mean, it relates to warship Captain Milisic, that he did not remember issuing such an order. Let me explain one more thing now. Then we were confronted, and I quite simply said that's not true, and I said exactly what it was like. And he didn't say anything. And then later on, when we went out, while we were waiting for transportation to go back, we were on our own, and if you don't believe me, the Court can call Kandic. And he said to me, "Oh, Pere, I have a granddaughter in Split." And then it was all clear to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was all clear to you?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was clear to me that he could not tell the actual truth. That was clear to me. And I did not like the fact that I had to tell the truth. All my friends were Croats. Milisic was my best friend. But I could not lie in a court of law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This explanation given by Admiral Kandic, who also took part in the proceedings against Ivan Milisic as a witness, what he said to you after the trial, as you said, "Oh, Pere, I have a grandchild in Split." In relation to what did he say that? What did he mean by this sentence? What did he try to express?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... how does this man know what Kandic meant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you see the point, Mr. Rodic? It is speculative.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I'm going to rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did Admiral Kandic tell you, "Pero, you see, I have" --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Same objection.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Daughter. Daughter. Granddaughter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I had indicated objection. Same ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I heard that, and you've heard that there was an answer given. So I think we'd better leave that alone now, Mr. Rodic. You've probably got what you wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Handzijev, were you a witness to the fall of the helicopter in which General Cokic and warship Captain Djurovic were?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a witness when the helicopter fell, because it fell close to us. We were on the road leading to Cilipi, the motorway. And we had to run away when the helicopter fell because the Croatian forces that were retreating from the village of Komaja because our forces were advancing there and then they were walking towards us, towards the road leading to Cilipi. And then we had to go away. We were in a small fiat, the small Fiat car, and we had to flee to Kupari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd like to object, Your Honour. The question was that he was witness to the fall of the helicopter. He said, if I remember the testimony, he was in the area of and he heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll move on, Your Honour, although the witness did describe this in greater detail during the cross-examination. Could the witness please be shown P119.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't have to read everything. Just look at this document, please, and tell us, in your view, what kind of a document is this?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a decision for further action. It is a decision of the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This decision was written on the 24th of October; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For which time period, to which time period does it relate? Does it pertain to that day or some other day?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, it pertains to that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does this mean, decision for further actions? When are these further actions carried out?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once an action is carried out, or when certain actions are envisaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In principle, combat orders and decisions for further actions of the command of the 2nd Operational Group, where were they sent to?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their command. It says here quite specifically, the 2nd Corps, the 37th VPS, the 9th VPS, and the 472nd Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the entire 9th VPS involved in military operations in the territory of Dubrovnik and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that we were a peacetime command. Our part did not participate in this, so we did not have to familiarise ourselves with these documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We no longer need this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described during your testimony work in the operations centre of the 9th Military Naval Sector in Kumbor and numerous activities that took place in that period towards the end of 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I am not referring to a precise piece of information now, but in view of these numerous activities, can you tell me approximately what the quantity of information was that came to your operations centre daily?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a great frequency involved. First of all, demands for additional personnel went through us as well, and we had officers who received that. We had two officers who were dealing with that. Then also when relocation started, we had lots of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Handzijev, you described these activities, relocation and communication with very many people. My question is: Can you somehow express this numerically? Are you talking about tens of pieces of information or hundreds?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hundreds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Also during your testimony, you explained what were all the things that were on the premises of the operations centre and, inter alia, you explained that there is communications equipment there and that there is also this desk with the telephone lines, this switchboard; is that right.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this desk with a switchboard, does it only have a receiver? And the person talking from that desk, can this person talk only through the receiver?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a speakerphone there, so that is a microphone, and also a receiver can be used. So it can be used as a telephone and as a speakerphone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any situations when calls and conversations would take place through this speakerphone, this Parlaphone, as you call it?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, speakerphone, Parlaphone. Sometimes they didn't switch it off. It depended on the person who was there on the desk. On the other hand, there can be another telephone line that is open at that moment, so...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the operations centre, were there several persons there?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes there would be several persons. Sometimes also the chiefs of arms and services would come there and they would have a conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, would this be the right time for the second break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at just after a quarter to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Handzijev, from Kumbor, from the operations centre at Kumbor, could you establish the military communication line with Cavtat and Mokosica?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Through the Kumbor operations centre, could you put through participants in Cavtat and Mokosica to another participant?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we could, through the forward communications centre. They had a small switchboard like we had. They would take up the line of communication and then they would put them through.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, pardon me. But a point of clarification. When a witness says "forward communications centre," could it be identified what is meant by that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Handzijev, can you tell us what this means, forward --

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said forward command post, the forward command post, IKM.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the command of the 9th VPS at Kumbor, was there a system in place for radio surveillance, eavesdropping on radio communications, more specifically?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not at Kumbor. In the building, there was a special body that was attached to us. They arrived from the PPO [as interpreted] command. That was the role they had, eavesdropping. That's where they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The transcript does not reflect the command you referred to. Which command? From which command did you receive those? If you could tell us the full name.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The VPO command. It was a section they had.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get the name that the witness referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those surveillance activities were not carried out from the operations centre at Kumbor?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The operations centre had nothing to do with that. They had -- had they had a direct line with them, they wouldn't have contacted us at all. But they didn't. But we were just some sort of transit. This was not our body. This was another body that existed earlier. They would coordinate, they would train, and they would be established up there at Obosnik. If they had a direct line of communication with them, they would have sent them messages, but they did it through us, because we were the switchboard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They also asked you a question about systems of surveillance at the operations centre of the 9th VPS in Kumbor. Can you tell us, please, from the operations centre at Kumbor, what specifically could you monitor or survey?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire situation, for example, at sea, when a ship was leaving the coast of Italy, for example, and then monitored the course of the journey. For example, what the speed of the boat was, what the crew was, what the course was that the boat had taken. It's the surface situation. That's how we referred to it. Vessels, ships, and planes too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what Voji is, V-o-j-i?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's air monitoring, air traffic monitoring. They had their own radars. There's a system of communication. They receive information from those radars, transfer them into a computer, and you get an idea what the situation in the area is like. The speed of a plane, at which a plane is travelling, the whole thing. It's a very sophisticated system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In order to avoid confusion: When you explained the conversation between General Kadijevic and Admiral Jokic, you used the expression "pair see and pair to," [phoen] didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I meant they were saying you to each other, second person singular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said about not remembering how General Kadijevic addressed Admiral Jokic, whether it was the familiar term of address or a more formal one, "vi," v-i, or "ti," t-i, in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I think he said plural or singular was the term used in the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're slipping back into giving the evidence yourself, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the question is about the grammar of B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You can ask the witness what he meant, rather than you telling him what he meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Handzijev, your uncertainty about the way General Kadijevic addressed Admiral Jokic, the form of address, what is your uncertainty about? Is it about whether General Kadijevic addressed him in the singular or in the plural?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I'm sure that he addressed him in singular. It was a more intimate form of address. That's how it is etched in my memory. Now I'm confused, in view of how much time has passed by since. It strikes me as illogical that they would. So that's why I have this dilemma. But I'm closer and closer to concluding that they addressed each other more intimately, in the singular form, second person singular. But I do have this dilemma.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe using your own words a relationship between two persons. Therefore, let us not think now specifically about Kadijevic and Jokic. When you talk to someone, when do you use the second person plural and when the second person singular? Can you please try to tell us what this would imply?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This question requires either an explanation in grammar or some area that is not necessarily within the explanation powers of this witness, or we haven't established that type of predicate, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Handzijev, do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, when you talk to a person, your decision whether you will address the person with the first person singular or the second person singular or the second person plural, what does that decision depend on?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm on intimate terms with a person, if we're close or familiar -- but even so, even if I'm on intimate terms with someone, if it's an official conversation, normally I would use the second person plural. However, if we're alone, we would use the second person singular. For example, the case of Zec. When we're alone, we use the second person singular. But if there's a third person present, I use the second person plural, the more formal form of address. If I understand you correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I believe you do. Thank you. At one point in time you mentioned, while explaining the situation with Kupari, between General Strugar and Admiral Jokic, you mentioned frustrations, the frustrations of Admiral Jokic. What exactly did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Speculative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No. He did express that. You didn't take any further your questioning as to the nature of that or what he meant by it. I would allow the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jokic was the secretary of national defence, and when the operations began, or rather, when unrest began in Yugoslavia, the riots, the women, the mothers, those whose sons were still in Slovenia when there were operations afoot in Slovenia, they went to the assembly and they requested answers from Jokic about when their sons would be back. I'm not sure what Jokic told them and how he explained the situation, but they attacked him with their umbrellas, with their brollies. They wanted him removed from his post, and that's when he was transferred and came to us. That is why I believed he was frustrated. Now that can be taken out of context, but in my opinion that is the explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Admiral Jokic say what he wanted, what he was after when he arrived in Kumbor?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know that there were several informal conversations, contacts, I had sporadically in our spare time, in a more relaxed atmosphere. Sometimes he would say, "Well, I'll have a cup of coffee on the Stradun." I certainly did hear him say that a number of times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Was this the first time you had Jokic as commander in October 1991, when he arrived in Kumbor?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had been my commander prior to that also, before he had left for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long have you known Admiral Jokic for?

utterances.speaker: PETRE HANDZIJEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite long. Since I arrived in the sector, that's when I believe I met him. He was the chief of the operations and training department for a while. He was the Chief of Staff. Well, he was the commander there, so I've known him for quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Handzijev, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this completes my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rodic. You'll be pleased to know that that concludes your evidence. You are now free to go and to return to your home. So thank you for coming and for the assistance you've given us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honours, for allowing me to contribute to the work of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, now that the testimony has finished, I would like to make two remarks, briefly. The first remark is I would like to have the tape of this testimony checked carefully when drawing up the final version of the transcript in relation to yesterday's and today's testimony, since a significant number of words - I did step in several times - but due to a lack of time, I omitted several interventions. Therefore, the tape needs checking so that we may have a complete testimony of this witness. Secondly, with the Chamber's permission, I would like to provide an explanation for the grammatical confusion that occurred in the last minutes of the witness's testimony, if I may, that is. From the point of view of the grammatical rules of B/C/S, the language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you have no need to do that. We grasp enough to follow. It's a feature that occurs in a number of languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Even French, I hear. Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we can proceed if you like. The Defence would like to call our next witness to take the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. And who is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovan Drljan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you take the card and read the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Rodic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, can you please tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: My name is Jovan Drljan. I am a frigate captain by rank and I am retired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us where and when you were born.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: I was born on the 9th of December, 1938, in the village of Luscani, Petrinja municipality, Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said you were a frigate captain, retired. Can you please try to compare that to an infantry rank.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: Lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Drljan, can you tell us about your educational background?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: Primary school in my native village, secondary school in Sisak and the military naval academy at Split, at the Divulje Training Centre of the navy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any occupational specialty or is that a more general kind of training?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: Later on I specialised for torpedoes and mines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of our conversation, since we speak the same language, could you please just pause briefly several seconds after I finish asking my question and then after this brief pause, you provide your answer. It's for the benefit of the interpreters and the transcript. Tell me, sir, please: From what time to what time were you serving in the army?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: As an active lieutenant colonel, between 1961 and the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in this period of time, which garrisons did you serve in?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: The one in Split. However, the destroyer on which I did an internship was being repaired in Rijeka, and I spent nearly a year in Rijeka, then briefly back in Split, after which I got a transfer to Sibenik. I spent 13 years in Sibenik and later got a transfer to Boka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when it was that you arrived in Boka?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: I arrived on the 1st of September, 1976.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you serve in the 9th Military Naval Sector?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: First I was the commander of the mine hunters in the village of Lepetane. That's where the command post was. I spent four years there. And in 1980, I arrived in the operations centre of the military naval sector of Boka. In the meantime, between 1984 and 1986, I had been sent to Libya, where I taught at the Libya naval academy. After that, I returned to the Boka Military Naval Sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you tell us about the second half of 1991. Where were you serving at that time and which position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: In the second half of 1991, I was serving in the Military Naval Sector of Boka at the operations and training department. I was there as an operations officer in charge of planning. All the sectors' plans that had to do with the unit's activities were drawn up by me, and I had an additional duty as a gym instructor throughout the sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991, did you work at the operations centre of the 9th VPS in Kumbor as a duty-officer?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: I was on the roster, as were a number of other officers, for operations duty at the operations centre, and I was one of those officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In late summer 1991, did you take part in any military activities outside Kumbor?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: On the 27th of September, I received an order from the late warship Captain Krstic, or rather, Krsto Djurovic, who then held the position of sector commander, to go to Pula, and pull out three patrol boats that were still based in Pula at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you were serving in the 9th Military Naval Sector, who at that time was your superior command?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: Our superior command at the time was the command of the military naval district, VPO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the military naval sector, in that period of time, did you receive orders from the command of the military naval district?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: Yes. We received orders from the command of the military naval district, just like in the case of this order, where I was ordered to go to Pula. This order had been issued by the command of the military naval district to the sector command, which then carried it out through my own group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Upon your arrival in Pula, did you carry out that task of moving the ships?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did, with a group of officers and NCOs, and we did manage to transport those ships to Boka. We stayed up there for repairs and maintenance of the machinery on board ship, to capacitate the ships for safe sailing, and they sailed to Boka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, if you remember correctly: When did you arrive in Boka Kotorska, the Bay of Kotor?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: We arrived in the Bay of Kotor on the 5th of October, at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: At that time, was the blockade of the Adriatic in force?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: The blockade of the Adriatic, to the best of my knowledge, from warship Captain Rakic, who was acting as a deputy of the Pula sector, I set sail on the 3rd, in the evening, at 2100 hours, and he warned me - I didn't see the order, but he did caution me - that the command of the military naval district had blocked the entire area of the Adriatic along our coast, our territorial waters, in fact, and that I should take care, that I should make myself known to the warships along the way so that they knew we were there and we wouldn't open fire at one another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you reached Kumbor, was the blockade still in force?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Do you know how long the blockade remained in force for?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: The blockade remained in force until -- I think it was the 11th of October, when an order came from the VPO, the military naval district.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did the order stipulate from the command of the military naval district? What was ordered?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: It was ordered that the blockade should be lifted for sailing in the Adriatic, which meant that vessels could move around but that they had to inform of them their movement. And this meant the whole coastline and the Dubrovnik area as well, the territorial waters there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to ask the usher to hand out a document now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I place an objection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We just received this document which learned counsel is about to show the witness. It's a document allegedly signed by Admiral Jokic, and it indicates that the Defence had this document during the period that Admiral Jokic was cross-examined, and it was never shown to the Admiral [indiscernible] and about this document, so there's a Rule 90(H) violation here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not necessarily. It depends on the nature of the document, whether it has to be shown. Can I see the document, please. I'll see it from Mr. Rodic, so I know I've got the right one. I've got two comments. I see no basis in the document for thinking that there is a problem that it wasn't specifically put to the Admiral. But I equally don't quite see what the document has to do with this case. But if you -- you will know more of your case than I would, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan, can you tell us whose document this is?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: This document is that of the command of the Military Naval Sector of Boka, Vice Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does the document refer to?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: The document refers to the deblocking of the -- to lift the naval blockade of the ports of the Dubrovnik municipality. He followed orders from the VPO, military naval district, and reduced the order for his area of responsibility, which means he deblocked Dubrovnik, and he mentions that the forces of the first and second ships of the 16th GMO should still be controlled. Continue to control the sea vessels, et cetera, et cetera, preventing the transport of weaponry and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: If I understood you correctly, since in the introduction to this document it says: "Pursuant to the order of the command of the military naval district," and then it has the number, "... of the 11th of October, 1991, I hereby order ..." Does that mean that this kind of order was issued by the command of the military naval district to the military naval sector of Boka, the bay of Boka?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: Yes, of course, on the basis of the command's orders. So he acted upon their order. It was written for our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now tell me, please, one more thing. Do to whom was this document and command addressed?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: It was addressed -- I'm not going to read it here, but it was addressed to the 16th GMO, which was engaged in enforcing the blockade and probably the battleship gunboat that was on the assignment at the forward command post in Kupari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you, Witness, at this point. There's no need for you to give us additional explanations or not to look at the document, and I have provided you with the document so that you can take a look at it and answer my question on the basis of that. So the 16th GMO, can you give us the full title?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: The 16th Border Naval Detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it in charge of carrying out the tasks with respect to the blockades and all the rest of it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To whom was this document also addressed? Take a look at the document, please, in order to answer the question. To which commands?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: The GMO, the operations centre, and the operational group, to the attention of the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like this Defence exhibit to receive a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be D105.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that period of time, that is to say, towards the end of summer 1991, up until the end of 1991, did the military naval district and the military naval sector carry out any other important activities during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: We were on the alert, on a state of readiness, all the commanding officers and units were at their positions in the barracks, until the activities started of refuting Croatian forces from the Prevlaka area, repulsing them. And I at the time was in Pula, however, but I heard when the operation started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: As to this period, the end of the summer to the end of 1991, were there any activities linked to any units of the military naval sector on the Adriatic coast in the Republic of Croatia, for instance, right up to Pula?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN
utterances.text: Yes.
